claims.text: At stage-0, NamingBefore.Calc and NamingAfter.TotalVnd do the same steps line for line (sum quantity × unit price over the lines, then take a tenth off when the bool is true); what changes is the names, plus the OrderLine record for the pair and a named constant for the 10.

NamingAfter.cs declares `private const int LoyaltyDiscountPercent = 10` where NamingBefore.cs writes the literal 10, and OrderLine holds Quantity and UnitPriceVnd where the tuple `(int q, int p)` holds q and p.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang@stage-0: Clean/NamingAfter.cs lines 3 and 9; Clean/NamingBefore.cs lines 7 and 17

claims.text: For a positional record such as `public sealed record OrderLine(int Quantity, int UnitPriceVnd)`, C# generates public properties named after the parameters, so the values are read as `line.Quantity` and `line.UnitPriceVnd`.
Other samples at stage-0 name their order-total methods TotalVnd too (WrongTotal.TotalVnd, LoggingDemo.TotalVnd).
By the C# naming conventions, types and methods are PascalCase and local variables and method parameters are camelCase; positional record parameters and constant names are PascalCase.

An ordinary two-slash `//` comment stays where it is written, not on the lines that use the name (every call of a method included); the compiler does not check what it says. The three-slash `///` kind is the one the compiler can read to build documentation.
claims.source_hint: C# spec, Lexical structure 6.3.1 'Comments'; refs/dotnet-docs/docs/csharp/language-reference/tokens/comments.md L8, L24

claims.text: `grep` searches files for lines that contain a pattern; given more than one file name, `grep -c PATTERN` prints one line per file: the file name, a colon, and the number of lines that match.
claims.source_hint: GNU grep manual, '-c/--count' and '-H' (file name prefix is the default with several files); verified by running in the stage-0 Clean folder

claims.text: In samples/DonHang.Samples/Samples/Clean at stage-0, `grep -c Vnd NamingBefore.cs NamingAfter.cs PlaceOrderSplit.cs` prints NamingBefore.cs:0, NamingAfter.cs:6, PlaceOrderSplit.cs:9 (the lesson says only 'above zero' for the last two).
claims.source_hint: run the command in examples/don-hang at tag stage-0

claims.text: PlaceOrderSplit.cs at stage-0 is the sample whose `Place` method places an order (checks it, totals it, then calls `Save` and `Notify`); it calls `NamingAfter.TotalVnd(lines, customerIsLoyal)` and declares methods named `Save` and `Notify`.
When a name will be read away from where it is declared, it should say what the thing is or does in the domain's words, so the reader does not need to open it.

As a default, unless the team already uses another form: yes/no values read as questions, methods as verbs, collections as plurals, single values and types as nouns; abbreviations and type prefixes make the reader decode.

When a name needs a comment to be understood, change the name and delete the comment; a long precise name beats a short vague one, which costs time for every reader who meets it away from the line that explains it.

When the team already has a word for a thing, keep it even if it breaks a shape rule; keeping that word matters more than any single naming rule. The lesson uses this to accept the noun TotalVnd as a method name.
A short name is fine when its whole use fits in a few lines and its meaning is plain, such as `i` counting through a short loop.
When a comment only explains what a value is, a better name is the fix for it.
At stage-0 nothing in the example repository calls NamingBefore.Calc; the only matches for `Calc(` and `NamingBefore` are in NamingBefore.cs itself.
